 Cite as: 610 U. S. ____ (2026) 1 
Per Curiam 
SUPREME COURT OF THE UNITED STATES 
No. 26A476 
FEDERAL COMMUNICATIONS COMMISSION v. 
SHERROD BROWN, ET AL. 
ON APPLICATION FOR STAY 
No. 26A477 
NATIONAL REPUBLICAN CONGRESSIONAL 
COMMITTEE, ET AL. v. SHERROD BROWN, 
ET AL. 
ON APPLICATION FOR STAY 
[October 14, 2026]
 PER CURIAM. 
On March 30, 2026, the Media Bureau of the Federal 
Communications Commission (FCC) issued a “public notice” about the FCC’s lowest unit charge (LUC) requirements. Those requirements, which are outlined in 47 
U. S. C. §315(b)(1)(A), concern favorable rates that broadcasters must charge for campaign advertisements in the
weeks leading up to elections. The notice stated that political candidates, joint fundraising committees with noncandidate members, and political parties engaged in coordinated political activity are entitled to the LUC.
Four candidates for Congress filed an application for review with the FCC, arguing that only political candidates 
are entitled to the LUC and asking the full Commission to
set aside the public notice as unlawful. Two months later, 
while their application was still pending before the Commission, the candidates filed a petition for review against

2 FCC v. BROWN 
Per Curiam 
the FCC and the United States in the Court of Appeals for 
the Fourth Circuit seeking the same relief. A divided panel 
of the Fourth Circuit determined that it had jurisdiction to
consider the candidates’ challenge, granted their petition,
and set aside the public notice. In doing so, the majority
reasoned that the plain text and legislative history of 
§315(b)(1)(A) limits the availability of the LUC to political
candidates. 
On September 4, 2026, we granted an application to stay 
the Fourth Circuit’s decision. In our per curiam opinion, we
explained that the Communications Act “makes clear” that
the Commission must resolve an application for review by 
order “before an aggrieved party may petition for further
review in federal court.” National Republican Congressional Committee v. Brown, 609 U. S. ___, ___–___ (2026) 
(slip op., at 2–3). “Because the candidates’ application for 
review was pending when they filed their petition for review,” we continued, “the Fourth Circuit likely lacked statutory jurisdiction to address their challenge.” Id., at ___ 
(slip op., at 3). Indeed, the Fourth Circuit’s holding to the 
contrary “split[] with every other Circuit to have considered 
the issue.” Ibid. (citing Council Tree Communications, Inc. 
v. FCC, 503 F. 3d 284, 287 (CA3 2007); Alabama Power Co. 
v. FCC, 311 F. 3d 1357, 1366 (CA11 2002); International 
Telecard Assn. v. FCC, 166 F. 3d 387, 388 (CADC 1999) (per 
curiam)).
Just one month later, on October 7, 2026, the same 
Fourth Circuit panel ordered the Commission to resolve the 
candidates’ application by October 9, 2026. The Commission thus had 48 hours from the entry of the Fourth Circuit’s mandamus order to issue its final decision. That, the 
Fourth Circuit believed, was “the only means to finally
move forward with . . . judicial review.” App. to Emergency
Application for Stay in No. 26A476 (CA4), ECF Doc. 30, p. 
18a, n. 2. The mandamus order came just one week after 
the Commission’s comment period on the candidates’

Cite as: 610 U. S. ____ (2026) 3 
Per Curiam 
application had closed, and in the midst of another comment period for a parallel application the Commission was
considering in tandem.
The FCC moved before this Court to stay the Fourth Circuit’s mandamus order. On October 8, 2026, the order was 
administratively stayed so that the Court could resolve the 
FCC’s application before the 48-hour deadline expired. 
To obtain a stay, the FCC must demonstrate “(1) a reasonable probability that four Justices will consider the issue sufficiently meritorious to grant certiorari; (2) a fair
prospect that a majority of the Court will vote to reverse the 
judgment below; and (3) a likelihood that irreparable harm 
will result from the denial of a stay.” Hollingsworth v. 
Perry, 558 U. S. 183, 190 (2010) (per curiam). In “close 
cases” we “balance the equities and weigh the relative
harms to the applicant and to the respondent.” Ibid. Each 
of these factors favors the FCC, so we grant the stay. 
A writ of mandamus is a “‘drastic and extraordinary’
remedy ‘reserved for really extraordinary causes.’” Cheney 
v. United States Dist. Court for D. C., 542 U. S. 367, 380 
(2004) (quoting Ex parte Fahey, 332 U. S. 258, 259–260 
(1947)). To obtain a writ of mandamus, a litigant must 
demonstrate that he has “no other adequate means to attain the relief he desires” and that his right to the writ is 
“clear and indisputable.” 542 U. S., at 380–381 (internal 
quotation marks omitted). Together, these prerequisites
ensure that mandamus, one of “the most potent weapons in
the judicial arsenal,” Will v. United States, 389 U. S. 90, 107 
(1967), is used only to correct a clear “‘usurpation of power’” 
by a lower court, id., at 95 (quoting De Beers Consol. Mines, 
Ltd. v. United States, 325 U. S. 212, 217 (1945)), or to compel an agency to “perform a ministerial or non-discretionary
act” over which the agency has “no discretion whatever.” 
Norton v. Southern Utah Wilderness Alliance, 542 U. S. 55, 
63–64 (2004) (internal quotation marks omitted).

4 FCC v. BROWN 
Per Curiam 
The Fourth Circuit’s decision to issue an “extraordinary”
writ was inappropriate under the circumstances. The Communications Act requires the Commission to act on every
application it receives, but it does not obligate the Commission to act within a particular timeframe. 47 U. S. C. 
§155(c)(4). The Commission may exercise its discretion to
set its own procedures and schedule for resolving such applications. See Vermont Yankee Nuclear Power Corp. v. National Resources Defense Council, Inc., 435 U. S. 519, 524 
(1978). Undeterred, the Fourth Circuit issued a mandamus 
order requiring the Commission to issue a final decision on 
the candidates’ application just five months after it was 
filed and within just 48 hours—all while the Commission’s
deliberation process was still ongoing. Our system of separation of powers does not allow the Judiciary to meddle in
“the workings of a coordinate branch of the Government” in 
this manner. INS v. Legalization Assistance Project of Los 
Angeles County Federation of Labor, 510 U. S. 1301, 1306 
(1993).
Finally, the FCC will suffer irreparable harm absent a 
stay. As discussed above, the Fourth Circuit’s mandamus 
order requires the FCC to issue a final order within just 48 
hours of its entry. To comply with the mandamus order, the
FCC must triage its ongoing deliberation process and prepare a final order on an extremely expedited timeline. That 
the mandamus order requires the FCC to abandon its deliberation process is itself an injury that cannot be remedied after the fact. The FCC thus satisfies the stay factors.
For the foregoing reasons, the Fourth Circuit’s order directing the Commission to abort its deliberative process and
issue a final decision on the candidates’ application for review in two days is stayed. 
* * * 
The application for stay presented to THE CHIEF JUSTICE 
and by him referred to the Court is granted. The October

Cite as: 610 U. S. ____ (2026) 5 
Per Curiam 
7, 2026 judgment of the United States Court of Appeals for 
the Fourth Circuit, case No. 26–2230, is stayed pending the 
filing and disposition of a petition for a writ of certiorari, if 
such a writ is timely sought. Should certiorari be denied, 
this stay shall terminate automatically. In the event that 
certiorari is granted, the stay shall terminate upon the 
sending down of the judgment of this Court. The related 
application for stay in NRCC v. Brown, case No. 26A477, 
presented to THE CHIEF JUSTICE and by him referred to the 
Court is denied as moot. 
It is so ordered.
 JUSTICE SOTOMAYOR and JUSTICE JACKSON would deny 
the applications.
